concepts.name: Kula vs. Gotra vs. Pravara: Distinctions and Functions
key_dimensions: Kula as patrilineal descent group vs. Gotra as exogamous lineage unit — definitional boundaries
Pravara as Vedic rishi lineage used in ritual contexts (marriage, sacrifice) — distinct from Gotra yet often confused
Role of Gotra in enforcing exogamy rules and its Brahmanical vs. Kshatriya application differences
UPSC trap: Pravara listed as sub-unit of Gotra in some texts vs. independent lineage marker

concepts.name: Sapinda Relationship and Its Legal-Ritual Implications
key_dimensions: Definition of Sapinda — shared 'pinda' (rice-ball offering) in ancestor worship, not merely blood relation
Sapinda as a marriage prohibition boundary — varying counts (7 generations paternal, 5 maternal in Dharmashastra)
Distinction between Sapinda prohibition and Gotra prohibition — overlap and where they diverge
Use in inheritance law (Mitakshara school) and how Sapinda hierarchy determined succession order

concepts.name: Joint Family System: Mitakshara vs. Dayabhaga Schools
key_dimensions: Mitakshara — birth-right in ancestral property; coparcenary includes sons, grandsons, great-grandsons
Dayabhaga (Jimutavahana) — ownership arises only at death of holder; no birth-right; Bengal/Assam prevalence
UPSC trap: Under Mitakshara, daughters were NOT coparceners until Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act 2005 — ancient text context vs. modern law distinction
Geographic distribution: Mitakshara = most of India; Dayabhaga = Bengal, Assam — examiner tests regional specificity

concepts.name: Patrilineal vs. Matrilineal Kinship Systems in Ancient India
key_dimensions: Patrilineal norm in Brahmanical Dharmashastra texts vs. evidence of matrilineal practices in Dravidian south (Nairs, Khasi antecedents)
Archaeological and textual evidence for matrilineal descent in certain tribal and proto-historic communities
Bilateral kinship in South Indian cross-cousin marriage systems — contrast with North Indian prohibitions
UPSC trap: Matriliny ≠ matriarchy — inheritance through mother's line does not imply female political authority

concepts.name: Exogamy and Endogamy Rules: Varna, Caste, and Gotra Intersections
key_dimensions: Gotra exogamy (must marry outside Gotra) vs. Varna endogamy (must marry within Varna) — simultaneous operation
Anuloma (hypergamy) vs. Pratiloma (hypogamy) unions — Dharmashastra approval/disapproval and offspring categories
Sapinda exogamy as a third layer operating alongside Gotra and Varna rules
UPSC trap: Anuloma was conditionally permitted; Pratiloma was strictly condemned — examiners test directionality

concepts.name: Coparcenary System and Property Rights in Joint Family
key_dimensions: Coparcenary as a narrower body within joint family — only male agnates within 4 degrees under Mitakshara
Concept of 'unobstructed heritage' (Apratibandha Daya) vs. 'obstructed heritage' (Sapratibandha Daya)
Women's Stridhan — its composition (gifts at marriage, from parents, husband) vs. joint family property
How partition (Vibhaga) dissolved coparcenary and the rules governing demand for partition by a coparcener

concepts.name: Anuloma and Pratiloma Marriages: Varna Hierarchy and Offspring Status
key_dimensions: Anuloma = higher Varna male + lower Varna female (tolerated); Pratiloma = lower Varna male + higher Varna female (condemned)
Specific offspring categories: Murdhavasikta, Mahishya, Ugra, Nishada, Ambashtha, Parasava — Manusmriti enumeration
How offspring Varna was determined — closer to father's or mother's Varna based on degree of transgression
UPSC trap: Examiners list mixed-Varna offspring and ask which parent combination produces them — requires memorization of specific terms

concepts.name: Eight Forms of Marriage (Vivaha) and Their Varna/Social Associations
key_dimensions: Brahma, Daiva, Arsha, Prajapatya (approved) vs. Asura, Gandharva, Rakshasa, Paishacha (unapproved/condemned)
Varna-specific prescriptions: Brahma ideal for Brahmanas; Rakshasa permitted for Kshatriyas; Asura associated with Vaishyas
Paishacha as the lowest form — by stealth/intoxication — its condemnation and yet its legal recognition in later texts
UPSC trap: Gandharva (love marriage by mutual consent) was not universally condemned — it was recognized for Kshatriyas; examiners test this nuance

concepts.name: Stridhan: Composition, Control, and Inheritance
key_dimensions: Components of Stridhan: Adhyagni (gifts at marriage fire), Adhyavahanika (gifts at departure), Pritidatta (gifts from love), Shulka (bride price)
Yajnavalkya vs. Manu on whether husband could use Stridhan — differing positions
Inheritance of Stridhan: daughters inherited before sons in some schools — UPSC trap vs. general property inheritance
Distinction between Stridhan and property received through inheritance (which was NOT Stridhan under most schools)

concepts.name: Gotra System: Origin Myths, Expansion, and Social Control Function
key_dimensions: Original 8 Gotras (Kashyapa, Bharadvaja, Vishvamitra, etc.) as Vedic rishi lineages — later expansion to hundreds
Gotra as mechanism of social control: prevented inbreeding while simultaneously consolidating Brahmanical identity
Non-Brahmin adoption of Gotra system — Kshatriya and Vaishya Gotras and their legitimacy questioned in texts
UPSC trap: Shudras and untouchables traditionally had no Gotra in Brahmanical texts — their kinship was organized differently

concepts.name: Niyoga: Levirate Practice, Its Regulation and Decline
key_dimensions: Niyoga = appointment of widow (or wife of impotent man) to cohabit with a designated man for procreation only
Vedic and early Dharmashastra sanction vs. later Smriti (Manu) condemnation — chronological shift in attitude
Strict rules: limited to 2 children, no emotional relationship, designated person usually brother-in-law (Devar)
UPSC trap: Niyoga ≠ widow remarriage — it was a specific procreative arrangement, not full remarriage; Manu condemned both but distinguished them

concepts.name: Cross-Cousin and Uncle-Niece Marriages: North-South Divide
key_dimensions: North Indian (Brahmanical Dharmashastra) prohibition on cross-cousin marriage as Sapinda violation
South Indian (Dravidian) system: cross-cousin marriage (especially mother's brother's daughter) as preferred/prescribed union
Uncle-niece marriage (especially elder sister's daughter) prevalent in South India — explicitly forbidden in North
Archaeological/inscriptional evidence from South Indian dynasties (Satavahanas) for cross-cousin and uncle-niece marriages

concepts.name: Widow Remarriage and Norms of Widowhood Across Varnas
key_dimensions: Vedic evidence suggesting widow remarriage was practiced (Atharvaveda references) vs. later Smriti prohibition
Varna differentiation: Brahmin widows most strictly prohibited; Shudra widows permitted to remarry in most texts
Sati (Sahagamana) — textual mentions in later Smritis vs. archaeological evidence; NOT universally prescribed in ancient texts
UPSC trap: Rig Vedic reference (10.18.8) interpreted as widow remarriage vs. symbolic ritual — scholarly debate that examiners exploit

concepts.name: Joint Family as Economic Institution: Property, Labour, and Redistribution
key_dimensions: Joint family as unit of agricultural production — undivided land holdings and collective labour in agrarian economy
Dharmashastra rules on joint family debts — whether sons bound by father's debts (Avyavaharika vs. Vyavaharika debts)
Role of eldest male (Karta) as manager — powers and limitations; could not alienate joint property without consent
Joint family as social security net — its function in caring for widows, elderly, disabled members

concepts.name: Kuladevata and Kuladharma: Kinship, Ritual, and Religious Identity
key_dimensions: Kuladevata (family deity) as marker of kinship identity — different from Gotra but often used alongside it
Ancestor worship (Shraddha) as the ritual binding mechanism of joint family and lineage continuity
Kuladharma — family-specific duties and customs that could override general Varna duties in certain texts
How ritual functions (Shraddha, Sapindikarana) were used to include/exclude members from kinship group legally

concepts.name: Adoption (Dattaka) in Joint Family and Kinship System
key_dimensions: Purpose of adoption: ensuring male heir for ritual continuity (Shraddha) — primarily religious, not social welfare
Conditions for valid adoption: natural son preferred; adopted son cut ties with birth family under Mitakshara
Twelve types of sons (Dvadasha Putras) in Manusmriti — legitimate vs. adopted vs. other categories and their inheritance rights
UPSC trap: Under Dayabhaga, adopted son had fewer rights than under Mitakshara — school-specific variation tested by examiners

concepts.name: Varna vs. Jati: Conceptual Distinction and Kinship Implications
key_dimensions: Varna = 4-fold theoretical/ritual classification; Jati = actual endogamous occupational group — these are NOT the same
Kinship (marriage, inheritance) regulated by Jati in practice, not by Varna — Brahmanical texts vs. social reality gap
Multiple Jatis within one Varna — each with separate endogamy rules, Gotras, and kinship customs
UPSC trap: Varna system has textual prescription; Jati system has social practice — examiners test whether candidates conflate them

concepts.name: Ashrama System's Intersection with Joint Family and Kinship Duties
key_dimensions: Grihastha Ashrama as the only stage where kinship duties (marriage, procreation, ancestor rites) were fully operative
Tension between Vanaprastha/Sannyasa (renunciation of family) and joint family obligations — Dharmashastra resolutions
Son's duty to perform Shraddha as the primary justification for son-preference and kinship continuity norms
UPSC trap: A Sannyasi technically exited the kinship system — he could not inherit, perform Shraddha, or be a coparcener — an often-tested exception

concepts.name: Women's Position in Joint Family: Rights, Restrictions, and Agency
key_dimensions: Manu's dictum on women's perpetual dependence (father → husband → son) vs. evidence of propertied women in inscriptions
Women as 'married out' of natal Kula — loss of membership in birth kinship group and integration into husband's Kula
Devadasi and Nagar Vadhu systems as exceptions — women outside conventional joint family kinship structures
UPSC trap: Some texts (Arthashastra) gave women more rights (divorce, property) than Manusmriti — source-specific variation tested
